flagged.title: Act 1: Prophecies & Lady Macbeth
flagged.reason: The video incorrectly introduces, defines, and labels Macbeth's Act 1 Scene 3 aside ('Two truths are told') as a soliloquy, which misinforms students on essential GCSE English Literature dramatic terminology (AO2).

mark_affecting.quote: Shakespeare uses a soliloquy... It's a speech where a character speaks their thoughts out loud while completely alone on stage... In this first soliloquy, Macbeth practically confesses...

flagged.title: Character Analysis
flagged.reason: The narrator repeatedly refers to Macbeth as 'Macduff', claiming that Macduff attends 'Macduff's coronation' and that 'Macduff leans entirely into toxic tyranny', which completely confuses the protagonist and antagonist and would severely cost marks in an exam.

mark_affecting.video_says: ...bravely refuses to attend Macduff's coronation. Macduff and Macduff present two wildly different versions of what it means to be a powerful man. Macduff leans entirely into toxic tyranny...
mark_affecting.lesson_says: Macduff refuses to attend Macbeth's coronation, and Macbeth (contrasted with Macduff) represents toxic tyranny and unrepentant violence.

flagged.title: Key Themes & Exam Technique
flagged.reason: The video explicitly defines AO4 as historical context and instructs students to include a dedicated context step to gain AO4 marks on a question where context is not assessed and AO4 actually assesses technical writing accuracy.

mark_affecting.quote: you absolutely must include context. That's your AO4... This is exactly where you secure those AO4 marks by proving how the Jacobean audience would have reacted
heavily embed that all-important Jacobean context
